column3: Traditional Maya religion has existed for more than two and a half millennia as a recognisably distinct phenomenon, within the wider frame of Mesoamerican religion.
In the Late Preclassic period stone inscriptions are made, and a mural of about 100 BCE shows an underworld figure linked with caves.
In the Classic period the many kingdoms practise rituals of kingship, bloodletting and the worship of ancestors, and nobles make pilgrimages to caves such as Naj Tunich.
After 900 the Postclassic hieroglyphic books, the Dresden, Madrid and Paris codices, are made.
Around 1500 Chichen Itza draws pilgrims to its cenote and the Yucatec priesthood is hierarchically organised; Landa describes Yucatán about 1566.
After the conquest the religion merges with Roman Catholicism; the Tzeltal Rebellion of 1712 in Chiapas centres on the cult of the Virgin Mary.
In the late 19th century the 'Caste War' of eastern Yucatán revolves around a 'Talking Cross'.
Today the religion coexists with the Pan-Maya movement and Christianity, and daykeepers still use the 260-day calendar.

column6: The Maya religion is a recognisably distinct tradition from this time, spread over many indigenous kingdoms.
Noblemen from Classic kingdoms went on pilgrimage to its caves and had their visits recorded on its walls.
Pilgrims from the surrounding kingdoms came to its large cenote.
